newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Battle heats up for euro settlement business.
newsitem.headline: Battle heats up for euro settlement business.

text.p: The introduction of a single European currency could eliminate the need for settlement systems in every European country, and competition to be the top clearer of euro securities is heating up.

"If EMU happens we will see countries close down their settlement infrastructure," Geoffrey Wakem, director at international clearing and settlement institution Cedel Bank told Reuters at the International Securities Market Association (IMA) annual conference on Friday.
"The system might be reduced to two local European settlement providers," he said.

Cedel, as well as its competitor Euroclear, are also part of the battle to gain as much market share of settling euro-denominated securities as possible. They are up against central securities depositories (CSDs) across Europe.

Bankers involved in developing the new infrastructure to cope with European economic and monetary union (EMU), scheduled for January 1, 1999, said the European Monetary Institute (EMI) was planning to develop links between CSDs in Europe.

"The EMI appears to be opting for the idea of bilateral links, but may end up allowing Euroclear and Cedel to act as central depositories because there is so little time to set up the infrastructure," a senior European banker said.
"A lot of local systems are not worth having. There is an inevitable trend towards fewer CSDs, but it is slowed down because everyone in Europe wants to protect their own business," he said.

Luc Bomans, managing director and general manager at Euroclear, said: "If we are very efficient in settling euro securities there will be no economic justification in building bilateral links between the local CSDs."
"You could very well channel (euro securities) via Euroclear or Cedel," he said.
Euroclear and Cedel already clear and settle a large number of domestic instruments, but tend to get the business that involves at least one foreign counterparty.
Trades between two German investors, for example, tend to be cleared and settled by the German CSD.

The distinction between domestic and international securities will become less clear once European countries share the same currency, and in preparation domestic CSDs are already vying for Eurobond business denominated in their home currency.

"Global bonds are now issued not just with clearing by Euroclear and Cedel, but often also with clearing in local markets," Martine Dinne, managing director of the domestic securities division at Euroclear said.
"It will be up to the issuer, and investors, to decide where they want euro bonds to be cleared," she said.
But the need for radically different settlement systems might not arise if market flows remain similar to those now.
"Investors can trade the euro anywhere they like, but the question is where it will be settled," Wakem at Cedel said.

"If this happens within one geographic area, there is no problem because you can still use the domestic system. If cross-border trades remain at current levels, these would go through Euroclear and Cedel, as they do now," he said.
"(But) there are already two cross-border settlement agencies with well-established electronic links and there is an argument to focus all (euro) activity there," Wakem said.
A report commissioned by ISMA and released at the conference, said the chances of settlement failures when the euro is introduced in 1999 were around 20 percent.
ISMA called on European governments to sort out practical issued as soon as possible so that banks could get their systems set up to cope with the euro.
The report analysed the impact of EMU on the repo market, worth $25 trillion in 1996.

"If there are problems in the euro's infrastructure, they are likely to be seen first in the repo market, because it is a relatively short-maturity and securities-settlement-intensive market," it said.
